# LLMPsych native site deployment

Derived from GG's installed Sites driver at `a8133d938c0aeaef462dc8c47819609669d3525c`.
The additional protected policy fields `name_prefix` and `hostname_suffix` prevent
LLMPsych declarations from colliding with other GG services or domains. The remaining
protocol is unchanged: repository `deploy/sites/NAME/site.yaml` declarations, native
credentialless builds, protected DNS/TLS/systemd provisioning, exact-revision health
and rollback through the existing harness release engine.

The private world has no website target. Product repositories may declare sites in
their assigned namespace; no site is created merely by enabling a target. The existing
`llmpsych.com` GitHub Pages site keeps its release owner. New Hetzner sites use the
LLMPsych namespace within GG's existing DNS zone, `llmpsych.1puni.com`.

## Agent-help deployment handoff

Checked 5 October 2026 for the Thursday 8 October demo. Application and declarations
belong to `llmpsych/landing`; this repository owns the scoped hosting adapter and
operator installation sources. This is a source-supported contract, not evidence
that help is deployed or that the deadline is assured.

### Hostname and release contract

The existing [landing policy](policies/landing.yaml) supports
`help.web.llmpsych.1puni.com`. Neither `help.llmpsych.com` nor
`help.llmpsych.1puni.com` passes its hostname restriction. The existing
`web.llmpsych.1puni.com` landing page uses port 8500. For the help service, landing
can use directory name `llp-web-help` and candidate port 8501 after checking its
complete declaration set and operator-confirmed port availability. This is not a
port reservation or an additional declaration in this repository.

| Field in landing's `deploy/sites/llp-web-help/site.yaml` | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `hostname` | `help.web.llmpsych.1puni.com` |
| `port` | Unoccupied port in inclusive range 8500–8519; candidate 8501 |
| `kind` | `service` |
| `runtime` | `python3.12` (`/opt/1puni-sites/bin/python3.12`) or `node` (`/usr/bin/node`) |
| `workdir` | Relative release directory; defaults to `.` |
| `argv` | Argument list appended to the selected interpreter; landing supplies its entry point and explicit loopback bind/port |
| `health` | Plain absolute HTTP path, default `/healthz` |
| `build` | Optional argument list, credentialless build, maximum 1800 seconds |

The directory determines the site name, which must begin `llp-web-` and be at most
21 characters. Unknown declaration fields are rejected. No arbitrary environment,
secret, volume, alternate identity or model-provider binding is supported. The
unit does not inject `PORT` or a release SHA. Bind to `127.0.0.1` explicitly;
nginx terminates HTTPS and forwards to the declared loopback port. The proxy
sets Host, X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For, supports upgrade headers and a
one-hour read timeout. It does not itself implement authentication, request quotas,
application session controls or a model access boundary.

Builds operate on an exported committed tree, without `.git`. They may add
self-contained regular files such as dependencies under `vendor`, but cannot
modify/remove committed files or include symlinks/special files. Do not use an
absolute-path or symlinked virtualenv artifact. Python gets workdir and release
`vendor` on PYTHONPATH. Prefer no build for a standard-library-only service.

The normal controller path publishes the accepted exact landing commit, then
converges `landing-sites`; landing also has a separate `landing-pages` target.
Keep the existing landing declaration and Pages behavior intact. A target with
no declarations can report ready without hosting anything. Do not run installation
scripts, the target's `apply`/`worker`, or manual provisioning as a substitute for
controller publication. Application readiness needs the evidence below.

### Sessions and model access

Each service runs as `site-NAME`, with private mode-0700 persistent
`/var/lib/llmpsych-sites/NAME` supplied as both `HOME` and `SITE_STATE`.
For help that is `/var/lib/llmpsych-sites/llp-web-help`. The release under
`/opt/llmpsych-sites/llp-web-help/releases/SHA` is immutable. The unit uses
ProtectSystem=strict, ProtectHome=true, PrivateTmp=true, NoNewPrivileges=true,
a private umask, and grants writes to the site state directory. Put durable
sessions there, not in the release, current link or temporary directory.

This is single-host persistent storage, not a managed database, backup, retention
policy or multi-host replication. SQLite or files need application-level ownership,
locking and session isolation. Landing must define expiry/deletion, protect session
identifiers and use secure cookies when applicable. State persists across restart,
upgrade and code rollback; incompatible migrations need a separately approved
backup/restore plan. Do not place participant data in Git, health responses or
release evidence. Synthetic sessions suffice for deployment verification.

**Live model access remains unestablished.** The documented shared Claude/Codex
logins authorize native steward agents, not this new service identity. Do not
copy/mount those credentials, run the service as the agent, or expose controller
execution as an application API. The declaration and generated unit contain no
supported application credential injection or scoped model broker capability.
A runtime interpreter and network connectivity alone do not authorize model use.

Operator action for a live model demo: identify and authorize an application-scoped
provider capability or an existing bounded broker, specify allowed model/use,
spend/rate limits and data handling, and have its owning runtime implement and
verify a supported protected binding for this site identity. Credentials must not
enter repository files, build artifacts or argv. This handoff does not authorize
that implementation or assert a broker exists. Until then, landing can provide an
explicitly labelled non-live walkthrough if acceptable to the operator; that does
not satisfy a claim of live model-backed help.

### Served revision and rollback

For a service, `/healthz` must return HTTP 200 with JSON containing `sha`, `release`,
`version` or `commit` equal to the exact 40-character lowercase Git commit. Capture
the running release identity at startup from the resolved immutable source path
(or a verifiable build identity). Do not read the moving `current` symlink on every
request or echo a caller's expected revision: an old process could then claim new
code. A plain 200 or product version is insufficient. The default health wait is
180 seconds. Loopback health does not prove public DNS/TLS or a user journey.

Before calling help ready, retain these non-sensitive facts for the same accepted
landing SHA:

1. Publication receipt and `landing-sites` observation naming that exact SHA and
   the actual help site, with no blocked declaration.
2. Current release resolves to that SHA; the service's loopback health reports it.
3. Public `https://help.web.llmpsych.1puni.com/healthz` has valid TLS, returns 200
   and reports the same SHA; fetch the UI over the same origin.
4. A synthetic session completes the advertised workflow; two sessions stay
   isolated, and promised persistence survives a controlled service restart.
   A live-model claim additionally requires an authorized call from the actual
   site identity, not a successful native steward login.

The existing engine restores and verifies the last healthy release after failed
activation/health. A failed first release removes the current pointer and stops
the service. Failed SHAs remain condemned; publish a corrected commit through the
normal path rather than manually clearing markers. For a deliberate application
rollback, revert the offending application change in landing and let the new exact
commit pass the usual gates and deployment checks.

Rollback does **not** reverse session writes/migrations, DNS, certificates, nginx
routing or generated unit configuration. Provisioning happens before release
activation. Preserve hostname, port, runtime and state compatibility for ordinary
application updates. Removing a declaration does not deprovision its resources.
Infrastructure changes require their own operator-owned restoration plan.

### Custom-domain cutover prerequisites

`llmpsych.com` remains owned by GitHub Pages; help is a separate subdomain. A CNAME
to the fallback alone is insufficient: existing TLS certificates, SNI routing and
hostname policy do not cover `help.llmpsych.com`.

Before offering that custom hostname, the operator and hosting owner must:

- Authorize exactly the additional hostname and establish zone control and a
  suitable protected DNS capability. The current policy allows zone `1puni.com`
  and one hostname suffix only. Merely adding `llmpsych.com` to `zones` still fails
  the suffix check; replacing the suffix would reject the existing landing site.
  A narrowly scoped change in the existing hosting system must preserve both
  declarations. No such policy/schema change is prepared or installed here.
- Record existing help A/AAAA/CNAME and relevant CAA/HTTP-01 conditions, preserving
  apex/www Pages and unrelated MX/TXT records. The current driver expects an
  unproxied A record to `204.168.179.65`; conflicting aliases, IPv6 or proxied
  records are refused. Confirm public HTTP-01 reachability for certbot and public
  HTTPS/SNI routing. Domain ownership and DNS-token access are not verified here.
- Decide whether fallback and custom names must coexist. A declaration supports
  one hostname and sites cannot share a port within a repository. Aliases are not
  an existing field; do not invent a second service/state store to fake one.
- Establish the fallback deployment first, then use the approved controller and

  exact served SHA, session/cookie origin behavior and a synthetic user journey

- Retain prior DNS/routing/policy/unit settings and the fallback's healthy SHA.
  If cutover fails, the owning operator restores those settings through the
  existing hosting procedure and rechecks fallback health and public access.

## Exact proposed binding

[50-model.conf](50-model.conf) is a source-only candidate for
`/etc/systemd/system/site-llp-web-help.service.d/50-model.conf`, root-owned 0644
in root-owned 0755 directories. It adds a required read-only bind mount and
suppresses core dumps for this unit only. No optional `-` prefix: missing source
must prevent service startup when this binding is installed.

The one canonical input is `/etc/llmpsych-sites/llp-web-help/runtime.json`:

- Parent directories root-owned 0700, no symlinks; regular file, mode 0400,
  owned by the resolved UID of `site-llp-web-help`. Root controls creation and
  replacement through the inaccessible parent; the service cannot reach the
  source pathname. Do not reuse that UID for unrelated processes/services.
- The mount exposes that inode read-only at
  `/var/lib/llmpsych-sites/llp-web-help/runtime.json` inside this unit's mount
  namespace. Mode 0400 satisfies the current reader; group-readable 0440 would
  fail it. The runtime must verify UID mapping and read-only enforcement.
- Prepare an empty regular root-owned 0400 destination placeholder while the
  service is stopped. Reject symlinks/special files at source, target and parents;
  do not overwrite an existing runtime input without an explicit migration review.
  Keep state directory ownership/mode as the existing site identity/0700.
- The JSON contains the dedicated provider key, approved model identifier and
  independently generated pilot access code. No example secret or populated JSON
  belongs in Git. This mount is not a backup or a second configuration writer.

The base unit already has `ProtectSystem=strict`, `ProtectHome=true`,
`NoNewPrivileges=true`, `PrivateTmp=true`, and grants state-directory writes.
The owner must verify the nested file remains read-only under that writable state
directory. The rest of the state remains writable for sessions. `ensure_unit`
replaces only the main unit file, so a separately owned drop-in is the minimal
integration point; no harness patch or installed harness edit is needed.
Retain this proposal here for the runtime owner rather than adding an installer
or pretending this repository controls protected runtime configuration.

## Authorized-owner installation and lifecycle (not executed)

1. Obtain approval for the decision below. Pin the accepted landing and runtime
   revisions; confirm exact site identity, fallback, state path, port, existing
   unit/drop-ins and no conflicting binding. Record prior non-secret configuration.
2. Through the owner's protected input channel, create the dedicated config outside
   Git and build/export trees. Never pass its values via shell arguments, environment,
   chat, shell history, stdout or logs. Use a protected editor/input facility; do not
   print the file. No native agent credentials, copying from native auth stores,
   account creation or provider purchase is authorized by this proposal.
3. Stop only the help unit; check paths and identity; prepare the placeholder and
   install the exact drop-in through the owning runtime's approved procedure.
   Reload unit definitions and start only help. This is a future installation
   sequence, not authorization to manually deploy application code.
4. Perform the boundary checks below before declaring the binding effective. Deploy
   accepted application revisions only through normal controller publication.
5. Rotate by atomically replacing the source file within the protected directory,
   restoring owner/mode, then restarting only help. A running bind mount and the
   application's cached config retain the old value until restart. Verify the new
   capability before revoking the old one, unless emergency revocation is required.
6. For rollback stop help, restore the previous protected file/drop-in metadata and
   restart after daemon reload as appropriate. For removal, stop help, remove only
   this drop-in and the known empty placeholder, reload and restart to obtain the
   application's absent-config behavior. A leftover empty JSON file causes startup
   failure; do not mistake it for absent configuration. Revoke the dedicated provider
   capability through its owner. Remove protected inputs using that owner's policy.

Do not delete or chown the state tree, sessions/database, release directories,
current pointer, other drop-ins, DNS/TLS/nginx settings or another unit. Application
rollback does not undo binding changes, provider calls or session writes. No schema
migration is proposed. Keep old credentials only within the operator's protected
rollback window; revoke after success. Backups of session state must exclude
`runtime.json`, especially if taken inside the service namespace. Root and the
application process can access the key: this protects distribution and mutation,
not against malicious code running as the authorized application identity.

## Verification and approval boundary

Before installation, source checks can establish the JSON reader behavior and
unchanged policy scope with synthetic values. They cannot establish mount/UID
isolation. On the owning runtime, first use a dummy file and verify:

- The actual help identity reads the mounted file, cannot overwrite, unlink or
  chmod it, and can still write a synthetic session. A different site UID and a
  credentialless build cannot read the protected source or mounted content.
- Required source missing causes unit startup failure; no installed binding plus
  absent config denies live requests. Invalid JSON/permissions fail closed without
  values in logs. Rotation plus restart changes the selected dummy configuration.
- Other units' effective definitions and synthetic help state are unchanged after
  installation and rollback. No credential values enter argv, unit Environment,
  build output, Git, health responses, logs or retained verification evidence.

After approval and actual credential installation, verify one bounded synthetic
provider call from the actual help service, with the approved model and configured
limits. Readiness flags only establish config presence, not usable model access.
Use the existing hosting README's exact-SHA, public TLS and session-isolation
checks before any live-service claim. Retain revisions, outcomes and sanitized
failure categories only; never provider bodies, keys, pilot codes or session text.

Minimum operator decision: approve OpenAI HTTPS with a specific compatible model
and a dedicated application capability; specify a spend ceiling, rate/use limits,
allowed pilot users and data constraints (what may leave the host, retention and
region requirements); identify and authorize the owning runtime to install this

a file mount does not enforce cost or egress policy, and `store: false` alone does

# LLMPsych native site deployment

Derived from GG's installed Sites driver at `a8133d938c0aeaef462dc8c47819609669d3525c`.
The additional protected policy fields `name_prefix` and `hostname_suffix` prevent
LLMPsych declarations from colliding with other GG services or domains. The remaining
protocol is unchanged: repository `deploy/sites/NAME/site.yaml` declarations, native
credentialless builds, protected DNS/TLS/systemd provisioning, exact-revision health
and rollback through the existing harness release engine.

The private world has no website target. Product repositories may declare sites in
their assigned namespace; no site is created merely by enabling a target. The existing
`llmpsych.com` GitHub Pages site keeps its release owner. New Hetzner sites use the
LLMPsych namespace within GG's existing DNS zone, `llmpsych.1puni.com`.

## Agent-help deployment handoff

Checked 5 October 2026 for the Thursday 8 October demo. Application and declarations
belong to `llmpsych/landing`; this repository owns the scoped hosting adapter and
operator installation sources. This is a source-supported contract, not evidence
that help is deployed or that the deadline is assured.

### Hostname and release contract

The existing [landing policy](policies/landing.yaml) supports
`help.web.llmpsych.1puni.com`. Neither `help.llmpsych.com` nor
`help.llmpsych.1puni.com` passes its hostname restriction. The existing
`web.llmpsych.1puni.com` landing page uses port 8500. For the help service, landing
can use directory name `llp-web-help` and candidate port 8501 after checking its
complete declaration set and operator-confirmed port availability. This is not a
port reservation or an additional declaration in this repository.

| Field in landing's `deploy/sites/llp-web-help/site.yaml` | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `hostname` | `help.web.llmpsych.1puni.com` |
| `port` | Unoccupied port in inclusive range 8500–8519; candidate 8501 |
| `kind` | `service` |
| `runtime` | `python3.12` (`/opt/1puni-sites/bin/python3.12`) or `node` (`/usr/bin/node`) |
| `workdir` | Relative release directory; defaults to `.` |
| `argv` | Argument list appended to the selected interpreter; landing supplies its entry point and explicit loopback bind/port |
| `health` | Plain absolute HTTP path, default `/healthz` |
| `build` | Optional argument list, credentialless build, maximum 1800 seconds |

The directory determines the site name, which must begin `llp-web-` and be at most
21 characters. Unknown declaration fields are rejected. No arbitrary environment,
secret, volume, alternate identity or model-provider binding is supported. The
unit does not inject `PORT` or a release SHA. Bind to `127.0.0.1` explicitly;
nginx terminates HTTPS and forwards to the declared loopback port. The proxy
sets Host, X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For, supports upgrade headers and a
one-hour read timeout. It does not itself implement authentication, request quotas,
application session controls or a model access boundary.

Builds operate on an exported committed tree, without `.git`. They may add
self-contained regular files such as dependencies under `vendor`, but cannot
modify/remove committed files or include symlinks/special files. Do not use an
absolute-path or symlinked virtualenv artifact. Python gets workdir and release
`vendor` on PYTHONPATH. Prefer no build for a standard-library-only service.

The normal controller path publishes the accepted exact landing commit, then
converges `landing-sites`; landing also has a separate `landing-pages` target.
Keep the existing landing declaration and Pages behavior intact. A target with
no declarations can report ready without hosting anything. Do not run installation
scripts, the target's `apply`/`worker`, or manual provisioning as a substitute for
controller publication. Application readiness needs the evidence below.

### Sessions and model access

Each service runs as `site-NAME`, with private mode-0700 persistent
`/var/lib/llmpsych-sites/NAME` supplied as both `HOME` and `SITE_STATE`.
For help that is `/var/lib/llmpsych-sites/llp-web-help`. The release under
`/opt/llmpsych-sites/llp-web-help/releases/SHA` is immutable. The unit uses
ProtectSystem=strict, ProtectHome=true, PrivateTmp=true, NoNewPrivileges=true,
a private umask, and grants writes to the site state directory. Put durable
sessions there, not in the release, current link or temporary directory.

This is single-host persistent storage, not a managed database, backup, retention
policy or multi-host replication. SQLite or files need application-level ownership,
locking and session isolation. Landing must define expiry/deletion, protect session
identifiers and use secure cookies when applicable. State persists across restart,
upgrade and code rollback; incompatible migrations need a separately approved
backup/restore plan. Do not place participant data in Git, health responses or
release evidence. Synthetic sessions suffice for deployment verification.

**Live model access remains unestablished.** The documented shared Claude/Codex
logins authorize native steward agents, not this new service identity. Do not
copy/mount those credentials, run the service as the agent, or expose controller
execution as an application API. The declaration and generated unit contain no
supported application credential injection or scoped model broker capability.
A runtime interpreter and network connectivity alone do not authorize model use.

Operator action for a live model demo: identify and authorize an application-scoped
provider capability or an existing bounded broker, specify allowed model/use,
spend/rate limits and data handling, and have its owning runtime implement and
verify a supported protected binding for this site identity. Credentials must not
enter repository files, build artifacts or argv. This handoff does not authorize
that implementation or assert a broker exists. Until then, landing can provide an
explicitly labelled non-live walkthrough if acceptable to the operator; that does
not satisfy a claim of live model-backed help.

### Served revision and rollback

For a service, `/healthz` must return HTTP 200 with JSON containing `sha`, `release`,
`version` or `commit` equal to the exact 40-character lowercase Git commit. Capture
the running release identity at startup from the resolved immutable source path
(or a verifiable build identity). Do not read the moving `current` symlink on every
request or echo a caller's expected revision: an old process could then claim new
code. A plain 200 or product version is insufficient. The default health wait is
180 seconds. Loopback health does not prove public DNS/TLS or a user journey.

Before calling help ready, retain these non-sensitive facts for the same accepted
landing SHA:

1. Publication receipt and `landing-sites` observation naming that exact SHA and
   the actual help site, with no blocked declaration.
2. Current release resolves to that SHA; the service's loopback health reports it.
3. Public `https://help.web.llmpsych.1puni.com/healthz` has valid TLS, returns 200
   and reports the same SHA; fetch the UI over the same origin.
4. A synthetic session completes the advertised workflow; two sessions stay
   isolated, and promised persistence survives a controlled service restart.
   A live-model claim additionally requires an authorized call from the actual
   site identity, not a successful native steward login.

The existing engine restores and verifies the last healthy release after failed
activation/health. A failed first release removes the current pointer and stops
the service. Failed SHAs remain condemned; publish a corrected commit through the
normal path rather than manually clearing markers. For a deliberate application
rollback, revert the offending application change in landing and let the new exact
commit pass the usual gates and deployment checks.

Rollback does **not** reverse session writes/migrations, DNS, certificates, nginx
routing or generated unit configuration. Provisioning happens before release
activation. Preserve hostname, port, runtime and state compatibility for ordinary
application updates. Removing a declaration does not deprovision its resources.
Infrastructure changes require their own operator-owned restoration plan.

### Custom-domain cutover prerequisites

`llmpsych.com` remains owned by GitHub Pages; help is a separate subdomain. A CNAME
to the fallback alone is insufficient: existing TLS certificates, SNI routing and
hostname policy do not cover `help.llmpsych.com`.

Before offering that custom hostname, the operator and hosting owner must:

- Authorize exactly the additional hostname and establish zone control and a
  suitable protected DNS capability. The current policy allows zone `1puni.com`
  and one hostname suffix only. Merely adding `llmpsych.com` to `zones` still fails
  the suffix check; replacing the suffix would reject the existing landing site.
  A narrowly scoped change in the existing hosting system must preserve both
  declarations. No such policy/schema change is prepared or installed here.
- Record existing help A/AAAA/CNAME and relevant CAA/HTTP-01 conditions, preserving
  apex/www Pages and unrelated MX/TXT records. The current driver expects an
  unproxied A record to `204.168.179.65`; conflicting aliases, IPv6 or proxied
  records are refused. Confirm public HTTP-01 reachability for certbot and public
  HTTPS/SNI routing. Domain ownership and DNS-token access are not verified here.
- Decide whether fallback and custom names must coexist. A declaration supports
  one hostname and sites cannot share a port within a repository. Aliases are not
  an existing field; do not invent a second service/state store to fake one.
- Establish the fallback deployment first, then use the approved controller and
  hosting installation process for any authorized change. Verify public TLS,
  exact served SHA, session/cookie origin behavior and a synthetic user journey
  again on the custom name before advertising it.
- Retain prior DNS/routing/policy/unit settings and the fallback's healthy SHA.
  If cutover fails, the owning operator restores those settings through the
  existing hosting procedure and rechecks fallback health and public access.
  DNS restoration is subject to caching; engine code rollback alone is insufficient.

and rollback through the existing harness release engine.

their assigned namespace; no site is created merely by enabling a target. The existing
`llmpsych.com` GitHub Pages site keeps its release owner. New Hetzner sites use the
LLMPsych namespace within GG's existing DNS zone, `llmpsych.1puni.com`.

belong to `llmpsych/landing`; this repository owns the scoped hosting adapter and
operator installation sources. This is a source-supported contract, not evidence
that help is deployed or that the deadline is assured.

### Hostname and release contract

The existing [landing policy](policies/landing.yaml) supports
`help.web.llmpsych.1puni.com`. Neither `help.llmpsych.com` nor
`help.llmpsych.1puni.com` passes its hostname restriction. The existing
`web.llmpsych.1puni.com` landing page uses port 8500. For the help service, landing
can use directory name `llp-web-help` and candidate port 8501 after checking its
complete declaration set and operator-confirmed port availability. This is not a
port reservation or an additional declaration in this repository.

| Field in landing's `deploy/sites/llp-web-help/site.yaml` | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `hostname` | `help.web.llmpsych.1puni.com` |
| `port` | Unoccupied port in inclusive range 8500–8519; candidate 8501 |
| `kind` | `service` |
| `runtime` | `python3.12` (`/opt/1puni-sites/bin/python3.12`) or `node` (`/usr/bin/node`) |
| `workdir` | Relative release directory; defaults to `.` |
| `argv` | Argument list appended to the selected interpreter; landing supplies its entry point and explicit loopback bind/port |
| `health` | Plain absolute HTTP path, default `/healthz` |
| `build` | Optional argument list, credentialless build, maximum 1800 seconds |

The directory determines the site name, which must begin `llp-web-` and be at most
21 characters. Unknown declaration fields are rejected. No arbitrary environment,
secret, volume, alternate identity or model-provider binding is supported. The
unit does not inject `PORT` or a release SHA. Bind to `127.0.0.1` explicitly;
nginx terminates HTTPS and forwards to the declared loopback port. The proxy
sets Host, X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For, supports upgrade headers and a
one-hour read timeout. It does not itself implement authentication, request quotas,
application session controls or a model access boundary.

Builds operate on an exported committed tree, without `.git`. They may add
self-contained regular files such as dependencies under `vendor`, but cannot
modify/remove committed files or include symlinks/special files. Do not use an
absolute-path or symlinked virtualenv artifact. Python gets workdir and release
`vendor` on PYTHONPATH. Prefer no build for a standard-library-only service.

The normal controller path publishes the accepted exact landing commit, then
converges `landing-sites`; landing also has a separate `landing-pages` target.
Keep the existing landing declaration and Pages behavior intact. A target with
no declarations can report ready without hosting anything. Do not run installation
scripts, the target's `apply`/`worker`, or manual provisioning as a substitute for
controller publication. Application readiness needs the evidence below.

### Sessions and model access

Each service runs as `site-NAME`, with private mode-0700 persistent
`/var/lib/llmpsych-sites/NAME` supplied as both `HOME` and `SITE_STATE`.
For help that is `/var/lib/llmpsych-sites/llp-web-help`. The release under
`/opt/llmpsych-sites/llp-web-help/releases/SHA` is immutable. The unit uses
ProtectSystem=strict, ProtectHome=true, PrivateTmp=true, NoNewPrivileges=true,
a private umask, and grants writes to the site state directory. Put durable
sessions there, not in the release, current link or temporary directory.

This is single-host persistent storage, not a managed database, backup, retention
policy or multi-host replication. SQLite or files need application-level ownership,
locking and session isolation. Landing must define expiry/deletion, protect session
identifiers and use secure cookies when applicable. State persists across restart,
upgrade and code rollback; incompatible migrations need a separately approved
backup/restore plan. Do not place participant data in Git, health responses or
release evidence. Synthetic sessions suffice for deployment verification.

**Live model access remains unestablished.** The documented shared Claude/Codex
logins authorize native steward agents, not this new service identity. Do not
copy/mount those credentials, run the service as the agent, or expose controller
execution as an application API. The declaration and generated unit contain no
supported application credential injection or scoped model broker capability.
A runtime interpreter and network connectivity alone do not authorize model use.

Operator action for a live model demo: identify and authorize an application-scoped
provider capability or an existing bounded broker, specify allowed model/use,
spend/rate limits and data handling, and have its owning runtime implement and
verify a supported protected binding for this site identity. Credentials must not
enter repository files, build artifacts or argv. This handoff does not authorize
that implementation or assert a broker exists. Until then, landing can provide an
explicitly labelled non-live walkthrough if acceptable to the operator; that does
not satisfy a claim of live model-backed help.

For a service, `/healthz` must return HTTP 200 with JSON containing `sha`, `release`,
`version` or `commit` equal to the exact 40-character lowercase Git commit. Capture
the running release identity at startup from the resolved immutable source path
(or a verifiable build identity). Do not read the moving `current` symlink on every
request or echo a caller's expected revision: an old process could then claim new
code. A plain 200 or product version is insufficient. The default health wait is
180 seconds. Loopback health does not prove public DNS/TLS or a user journey.

Before calling help ready, retain these non-sensitive facts for the same accepted
landing SHA:

1. Publication receipt and `landing-sites` observation naming that exact SHA and
   the actual help site, with no blocked declaration.
2. Current release resolves to that SHA; the service's loopback health reports it.
3. Public `https://help.web.llmpsych.1puni.com/healthz` has valid TLS, returns 200
   and reports the same SHA; fetch the UI over the same origin.
4. A synthetic session completes the advertised workflow; two sessions stay
   isolated, and promised persistence survives a controlled service restart.
   A live-model claim additionally requires an authorized call from the actual
   site identity, not a successful native steward login.

The existing engine restores and verifies the last healthy release after failed
activation/health. A failed first release removes the current pointer and stops
the service. Failed SHAs remain condemned; publish a corrected commit through the
normal path rather than manually clearing markers. For a deliberate application
rollback, revert the offending application change in landing and let the new exact
commit pass the usual gates and deployment checks.

Rollback does **not** reverse session writes/migrations, DNS, certificates, nginx
routing or generated unit configuration. Provisioning happens before release
activation. Preserve hostname, port, runtime and state compatibility for ordinary
application updates. Removing a declaration does not deprovision its resources.
Infrastructure changes require their own operator-owned restoration plan.

### Custom-domain cutover prerequisites

`llmpsych.com` remains owned by GitHub Pages; help is a separate subdomain. A CNAME
to the fallback alone is insufficient: existing TLS certificates, SNI routing and
hostname policy do not cover `help.llmpsych.com`.

Before offering that custom hostname, the operator and hosting owner must:

- Authorize exactly the additional hostname and establish zone control and a

  and one hostname suffix only. Merely adding `llmpsych.com` to `zones` still fails
  the suffix check; replacing the suffix would reject the existing landing site.
  A narrowly scoped change in the existing hosting system must preserve both
  declarations. No such policy/schema change is prepared or installed here.
- Record existing help A/AAAA/CNAME and relevant CAA/HTTP-01 conditions, preserving
  apex/www Pages and unrelated MX/TXT records. The current driver expects an

- Decide whether fallback and custom names must coexist. A declaration supports

- Establish the fallback deployment first, then use the approved controller and

- Retain prior DNS/routing/policy/unit settings and the fallback's healthy SHA.
  If cutover fails, the owning operator restores those settings through the
  existing hosting procedure and rechecks fallback health and public access.
  DNS restoration is subject to caching; engine code rollback alone is insufficient.

# Engineering doctrine

This is how the harness is built, and how anything working on it, human or
model, is expected to think. It is opinionated on purpose. Parts of it
contradict conventional "best practice", and they mean to. Do not quietly
swap the common habit back in because it feels safer. It isn't. It is just
more familiar.

> The smallest system that correctly represents reality is usually the most
> robust one.

Complexity is not robustness. Generality is not robustness. Defensive code is
not automatically robustness, and an abstraction is not automatically
architecture. Every concept you add has a cost, so it carries the burden of
proof.

## Do not model the mess

Model the structure that generated the mess.

The goal is not to reproduce accidental complexity faithfully. The goal is to
understand the underlying system well enough that the unnecessary complexity
disappears. A good solution feels more inevitable the better you understand
the problem. If it feels more *clever*, be suspicious.

Here is the test we like best. Write the whole machine as pseudocode, without
borrowing a single class, module or table name from the implementation. For
this harness it comes out at roughly a hundred lines: observe, derive the
desired state, execute, verify, commit. Now compare that with what is
actually implemented. Fifteen thousand lines implementing fifteen thousand
lines' worth of irreducible behaviour is fine. Fifteen thousand lines
implementing a hundred lines of idea is entropy.

And the uncomfortable corollary: **if 90% of a system is translating the same
underlying data into different shapes, the ratio itself tells you the system is
broken.** Nobody wrote that on purpose. It is what overzealous writing without
understanding looks like once it has had a few months to compound.

## Twelve principles

### 1. Find the natural taxonomy first

Before you implement anything, find out what kinds of things actually exist in
the problem. What are the fundamental entities? Which distinctions between them
are real, and which were invented by the current code? What belongs at the same
level, and what does not?

Existing code is evidence, not truth. If the problem has five meaningful ideas
and the implementation exposes fifty equally important concepts, assume the
abstraction is wrong until proven otherwise.

Then derive the architecture from constraints, not from patterns: trust boundaries,
ownership, lifecycle, information flow, irreversible actions, failure domains,
persistence and concurrency guarantees. Patterns can help once those are known;
they are no substitute for knowing them. Before substantial implementation you
should be able to say what the invariants are, which states are possible and which
impossible, where authority lives and where trust changes. After that, the
implementation should be unsurprising.

### 2. Reduce the state space before handling edge cases

For every branch and edge-case handler, ask: *can this situation physically or
logically occur, given the system's invariants?* If it cannot, delete the state
instead of handling it.

Prefer impossible states made unrepresentable, invalid transitions structurally
prevented, narrower types, narrower interfaces and smaller authority surfaces
over ever more sophisticated defensive logic. Robustness comes mostly from
reducing what the system is *capable* of doing wrong.

### 3. Complexity must justify itself

When code becomes hard to reason about, do not first ask how to organise the
complexity. Ask whether it should exist. Is the problem modelled wrongly? Are
impossible cases being represented? Are two concepts actually one? Is one
concept doing several unrelated jobs? Is historical baggage posing as a
requirement? Is the code reproducing the shape of an earlier implementation
rather than the shape of the problem? Can an invariant replace a branch, a
constraint replace an instruction, a deletion replace a subsystem?

Do not refactor bloat into more aesthetically pleasing bloat.

### 4. Keep essential complexity, attack the accidental kind

Some complexity belongs to reality: real concurrency, external failure modes,
protocol semantics, distributed state, security boundaries. Keep it. Pretending
it away is not simplification, it is a bug with good manners.

Everything else, attack: duplicated representations, adapters between things
that should already speak the same language, speculative abstractions,
defensive handling of impossible states, configuration that configures
configuration, and wrappers with no semantic responsibility. The goal is not
minimal code at any cost. It is minimal *accidental* complexity.

### 5. Prefer invariants over instructions

If something must never happen, do not rely on documentation, convention,
prompts or discipline to prevent it. Make it structurally impossible.
Permissions over warnings. Schemas over prose. Types over comments. Separate
processes over behavioural instructions. A rule that has to be remembered is
weaker than a system that cannot break it.

### 6. Separate intelligence from authority

> The model proposes. The harness disposes.

Reasoning capability and execution authority are different things. The model
may reason as broadly as it likes; its authority stays narrow, explicit and
enforced from outside. Gates, permissions, repository protection and deployment
controls live outside the model's discretion, and the model does not get to
weaken them because it can argue convincingly about them. Intelligence works
inside strong boundaries. It does not replace them.

Make those boundaries obvious: authority, ownership, where data enters, validation,
persistence, external effects, irreversible operations and trust transitions.
Centralise each where it can be understood and enforced, rather than spreading it
through the codebase, and keep things simple inside it.

### 7. Decompose by meaning, not by file size

A component deserves to exist when it owns one coherent concept, invariant or
transition. You should be able to describe it in one precise sentence. If the
description needs a paragraph of unrelated "and also"s, it is several
components wearing one coat. Many small files that leave the conceptual
coupling untouched are not decomposition. They are confetti.

### 8. Search upstream for the shared cause

When several symptoms appear, do not assume several bugs. Ask: *what is the
smallest upstream cause that explains the largest number of downstream
observations?* Several awkward implementations usually mean one wrong
abstraction. Several failures usually mean one broken invariant. If component B
is awkward because component A exposes the wrong concept, fix A and delete the
compensation in B.

### 9. Make the representation do the work

Choose data structures, schemas and state machines that make correct behaviour
the natural behaviour. A good representation *removes* code. If a lot of logic
exists only to interpret or repair the representation, the representation is
wrong. Keep one canonical form. Keep derived information derived. If two pieces
of state must be kept in sync, first ask why there are two, because the best
synchronisation mechanism is usually deleting one of them.

### 10. Do not add generality without evidence

No plugin systems for plugins nobody has written. No interface for its one
implementation. No configuration for a case nobody has. Generalise when two
real instances reveal their shared structure, not when one imagined future
consumer might appreciate it.

### 11. Treat existing code adversarially

Existing *behaviour* may be required. Existing *structure* is not. Separate
externally observable behaviour and genuine invariants from historical
workarounds and obsolete assumptions. Every existing abstraction has to keep
earning its place. Sunk effort is not an argument. Neither is a passing test,
because a test verifies the implementation we happened to build. It does not
prove that implementation should exist.

### 12. Global simplicity beats local elegance

A helper can be beautiful while the system is incoherent. The recurring failure
in software is making every component locally tidy, defensive, reusable and
complete while the whole becomes incomprehensible. Judge each decision at
repository scale. Does it add a concept, a source of truth, a lifecycle, an
authority holder, another place state can diverge? Or does it just move the
complexity somewhere you are not looking?

## The operating system already solved this

A mature operating system, filesystem, language runtime and version-control
system embody decades of work on composition, isolation, persistence,
concurrency and observability. Use them before building weaker copies inside
the codebase.

**The filesystem is a state primitive.** A file can be human-readable
configuration, machine-readable configuration, durable state, an audit
surface, a diff, a trigger and a synchronisation boundary, all at once, and
every ordinary tool already knows how to handle it. Do not hide a direct
filesystem transition behind three layers of repository classes because it
feels "low level". Read the file, transform the data, write the file, and
respect atomicity where it actually matters.

**Git is part of the state machine.** It is not a developer tool that sits
outside the application. A branch holds proposed state. A commit is an
immutable description of a transition. The diff says exactly what changed.
Integration is acceptance. The default branch is accepted desired state, and
deployment realises it. That gives you provenance, rollback, inspection,
ordering and synchronisation from machinery that already exists and already
works. Do not rebuild it in an application database because someone once said
"Git is not a database". Understand the guarantees and use them deliberately.

**Change the source of truth, not every consumer of it.** If changing the model
for a rhythm is conceptually a configuration change, it is a configuration
change: edit the YAML, commit it, let the normal path apply it. Not a runtime
override table, a model registry or a parallel control plane.

**Prefer the language.** In Python that means `functools`, `itertools`,
`collections`, `pathlib`, generators, context managers and the sort you
already have, before any home-made infrastructure. Think in transformations
where you can (input, filter, map, reduce, output) and keep explicit state for
the parts of reality that are actually stateful.

The [representation example](engineering-doctrine-example.md) walks through the
classic case: a task that wanted to be a database row, an ORM model, a status
column and a sync job, and turned out to be a file in Git.

## Before you delete anything, ask two questions

"If I delete this, what concrete required behaviour becomes impossible?" is the
right question. It comes too late if you skip these two.

**Is it an invariant at all?** Much of what a codebase enforces is a performance
wish, a tidiness habit or a fear, written in the grammar of a rule so nobody
argues with it. "A withdrawn task must stop its running gate" reads like
correctness. It isn't. The requirement is that withdrawn work must not *land*.
Whether the gate finishes first is a question about wasted CPU, and wasted CPU
is not an invariant.

**Does the representation already hold it?** An invariant can be held by
design or by code, and only one of those needs maintenance. If withdrawal is
checked by the one writer that can push, nothing else has to check it. The
same invariant held by a status column needs a predicate at every stage that
might act, plus a recovery pass for rows whose process died. That code is the
price of choosing a representation that does not hold the invariant.

An invariant that survives both questions gets code. One that fails the first
was never real. One that fails the second is telling you the fact lives in the
wrong place, so move the fact instead of writing the check.

## Demolish, then fill

We call this *stormbeslå*. It is the one method here we will defend against
anyone.

Do not refactor by editing small pieces. The failure is structural, not a lack
of discipline: a small edit has no constraint on its own size, so each one is
locally defensible while the total grows. That is exactly how a well-behaved
session leaves every commit green, every decision reasonable, and the source
seven hundred lines *larger* than it started.

So invert it. Pick a whole concept, not a convenient file. Delete it
everywhere: the store, the module, its callers, its synchronisation, its
recovery path and the tests that only protect that machinery. Leave a hole with
the replacement primitive written on the rim. Do that everywhere in the concept
before you fill anything. Now the holes are visible, the line count has already

# Engineering doctrine

This is how the harness is built, and how anything working on it, human or
model, is expected to think. It is opinionated on purpose. Parts of it
contradict conventional "best practice", and they mean to. Do not quietly
swap the common habit back in because it feels safer. It isn't. It is just
more familiar.

> The smallest system that correctly represents reality is usually the most
> robust one.

Complexity is not robustness. Generality is not robustness. Defensive code is
not automatically robustness, and an abstraction is not automatically
architecture. Every concept you add has a cost, so it carries the burden of
proof.

## Do not model the mess

Model the structure that generated the mess.

The goal is not to reproduce accidental complexity faithfully. The goal is to
understand the underlying system well enough that the unnecessary complexity
disappears. A good solution feels more inevitable the better you understand
the problem. If it feels more *clever*, be suspicious.

Here is the test we like best. Write the whole machine as pseudocode, without
borrowing a single class, module or table name from the implementation. For
this harness it comes out at roughly a hundred lines: observe, derive the
desired state, execute, verify, commit. Now compare that with what is
actually implemented. Fifteen thousand lines implementing fifteen thousand
lines' worth of irreducible behaviour is fine. Fifteen thousand lines
implementing a hundred lines of idea is entropy.

And the uncomfortable corollary: **if 90% of a system is translating the same
underlying data into different shapes, the ratio itself tells you the system is
broken.** Nobody wrote that on purpose. It is what overzealous writing without
understanding looks like once it has had a few months to compound.

## Twelve principles

### 1. Find the natural taxonomy first

Before you implement anything, find out what kinds of things actually exist in
the problem. What are the fundamental entities? Which distinctions between them
are real, and which were invented by the current code? What belongs at the same
level, and what does not?

Existing code is evidence, not truth. If the problem has five meaningful ideas
and the implementation exposes fifty equally important concepts, assume the
abstraction is wrong until proven otherwise.

Then derive the architecture from constraints, not from patterns: trust boundaries,
ownership, lifecycle, information flow, irreversible actions, failure domains,
persistence and concurrency guarantees. Patterns can help once those are known;
they are no substitute for knowing them. Before substantial implementation you
should be able to say what the invariants are, which states are possible and which
impossible, where authority lives and where trust changes. After that, the
implementation should be unsurprising.

### 2. Reduce the state space before handling edge cases

For every branch and edge-case handler, ask: *can this situation physically or
logically occur, given the system's invariants?* If it cannot, delete the state
instead of handling it.

Prefer impossible states made unrepresentable, invalid transitions structurally
prevented, narrower types, narrower interfaces and smaller authority surfaces
over ever more sophisticated defensive logic. Robustness comes mostly from
reducing what the system is *capable* of doing wrong.

### 3. Complexity must justify itself

When code becomes hard to reason about, do not first ask how to organise the
complexity. Ask whether it should exist. Is the problem modelled wrongly? Are
impossible cases being represented? Are two concepts actually one? Is one
concept doing several unrelated jobs? Is historical baggage posing as a
requirement? Is the code reproducing the shape of an earlier implementation
rather than the shape of the problem? Can an invariant replace a branch, a
constraint replace an instruction, a deletion replace a subsystem?

Do not refactor bloat into more aesthetically pleasing bloat.

### 4. Keep essential complexity, attack the accidental kind

Some complexity belongs to reality: real concurrency, external failure modes,
protocol semantics, distributed state, security boundaries. Keep it. Pretending
it away is not simplification, it is a bug with good manners.

Everything else, attack: duplicated representations, adapters between things
that should already speak the same language, speculative abstractions,
defensive handling of impossible states, configuration that configures
configuration, and wrappers with no semantic responsibility. The goal is not
minimal code at any cost. It is minimal *accidental* complexity.

### 5. Prefer invariants over instructions

If something must never happen, do not rely on documentation, convention,
prompts or discipline to prevent it. Make it structurally impossible.
Permissions over warnings. Schemas over prose. Types over comments. Separate
processes over behavioural instructions. A rule that has to be remembered is
weaker than a system that cannot break it.

### 6. Separate intelligence from authority

> The model proposes. The harness disposes.

Reasoning capability and execution authority are different things. The model
may reason as broadly as it likes; its authority stays narrow, explicit and
enforced from outside. Gates, permissions, repository protection and deployment
controls live outside the model's discretion, and the model does not get to
weaken them because it can argue convincingly about them. Intelligence works
inside strong boundaries. It does not replace them.

Make those boundaries obvious: authority, ownership, where data enters, validation,
persistence, external effects, irreversible operations and trust transitions.
Centralise each where it can be understood and enforced, rather than spreading it
through the codebase, and keep things simple inside it.

### 7. Decompose by meaning, not by file size

A component deserves to exist when it owns one coherent concept, invariant or
transition. You should be able to describe it in one precise sentence. If the
description needs a paragraph of unrelated "and also"s, it is several
components wearing one coat. Many small files that leave the conceptual
coupling untouched are not decomposition. They are confetti.

### 8. Search upstream for the shared cause

When several symptoms appear, do not assume several bugs. Ask: *what is the
smallest upstream cause that explains the largest number of downstream
observations?* Several awkward implementations usually mean one wrong
abstraction. Several failures usually mean one broken invariant. If component B
is awkward because component A exposes the wrong concept, fix A and delete the
compensation in B.

### 9. Make the representation do the work

Choose data structures, schemas and state machines that make correct behaviour
the natural behaviour. A good representation *removes* code. If a lot of logic
exists only to interpret or repair the representation, the representation is
wrong. Keep one canonical form. Keep derived information derived. If two pieces
of state must be kept in sync, first ask why there are two, because the best
synchronisation mechanism is usually deleting one of them.

### 10. Do not add generality without evidence

No plugin systems for plugins nobody has written. No interface for its one
implementation. No configuration for a case nobody has. Generalise when two
real instances reveal their shared structure, not when one imagined future
consumer might appreciate it.

### 11. Treat existing code adversarially

Existing *behaviour* may be required. Existing *structure* is not. Separate
externally observable behaviour and genuine invariants from historical
workarounds and obsolete assumptions. Every existing abstraction has to keep
earning its place. Sunk effort is not an argument. Neither is a passing test,
because a test verifies the implementation we happened to build. It does not
prove that implementation should exist.

### 12. Global simplicity beats local elegance

A helper can be beautiful while the system is incoherent. The recurring failure
in software is making every component locally tidy, defensive, reusable and
complete while the whole becomes incomprehensible. Judge each decision at
repository scale. Does it add a concept, a source of truth, a lifecycle, an
authority holder, another place state can diverge? Or does it just move the
complexity somewhere you are not looking?

## The operating system already solved this

A mature operating system, filesystem, language runtime and version-control
system embody decades of work on composition, isolation, persistence,
concurrency and observability. Use them before building weaker copies inside
the codebase.

**The filesystem is a state primitive.** A file can be human-readable
configuration, machine-readable configuration, durable state, an audit
surface, a diff, a trigger and a synchronisation boundary, all at once, and
every ordinary tool already knows how to handle it. Do not hide a direct

feels "low level". Read the file, transform the data, write the file, and
respect atomicity where it actually matters.

**Git is part of the state machine.** It is not a developer tool that sits

ordering and synchronisation from machinery that already exists and already

already have, before any home-made infrastructure. Think in transformations

# Engineering doctrine

This is how the harness is built, and how anything working on it, human or
model, is expected to think. It is opinionated on purpose. Parts of it
contradict conventional "best practice", and they mean to. Do not quietly
swap the common habit back in because it feels safer. It isn't. It is just
more familiar.

> The smallest system that correctly represents reality is usually the most
> robust one.

Complexity is not robustness. Generality is not robustness. Defensive code is
not automatically robustness, and an abstraction is not automatically
architecture. Every concept you add has a cost, so it carries the burden of
proof.

## Do not model the mess

Model the structure that generated the mess.

The goal is not to reproduce accidental complexity faithfully. The goal is to
understand the underlying system well enough that the unnecessary complexity
disappears. A good solution feels more inevitable the better you understand
the problem. If it feels more *clever*, be suspicious.

Here is the test we like best. Write the whole machine as pseudocode, without
borrowing a single class, module or table name from the implementation. For
this harness it comes out at roughly a hundred lines: observe, derive the
desired state, execute, verify, commit. Now compare that with what is
actually implemented. Fifteen thousand lines implementing fifteen thousand
lines' worth of irreducible behaviour is fine. Fifteen thousand lines
implementing a hundred lines of idea is entropy.

And the uncomfortable corollary: **if 90% of a system is translating the same
underlying data into different shapes, the ratio itself tells you the system is
broken.** Nobody wrote that on purpose. It is what overzealous writing without
understanding looks like once it has had a few months to compound.

## Twelve principles

### 1. Find the natural taxonomy first

Before you implement anything, find out what kinds of things actually exist in
the problem. What are the fundamental entities? Which distinctions between them
are real, and which were invented by the current code? What belongs at the same
level, and what does not?

Existing code is evidence, not truth. If the problem has five meaningful ideas
and the implementation exposes fifty equally important concepts, assume the
abstraction is wrong until proven otherwise.

Then derive the architecture from constraints, not from patterns: trust boundaries,
ownership, lifecycle, information flow, irreversible actions, failure domains,
persistence and concurrency guarantees. Patterns can help once those are known;
they are no substitute for knowing them. Before substantial implementation you
should be able to say what the invariants are, which states are possible and which
impossible, where authority lives and where trust changes. After that, the
implementation should be unsurprising.

### 2. Reduce the state space before handling edge cases

For every branch and edge-case handler, ask: *can this situation physically or
logically occur, given the system's invariants?* If it cannot, delete the state
instead of handling it.

Prefer impossible states made unrepresentable, invalid transitions structurally
prevented, narrower types, narrower interfaces and smaller authority surfaces
over ever more sophisticated defensive logic. Robustness comes mostly from
reducing what the system is *capable* of doing wrong.

### 3. Complexity must justify itself

When code becomes hard to reason about, do not first ask how to organise the
complexity. Ask whether it should exist. Is the problem modelled wrongly? Are
impossible cases being represented? Are two concepts actually one? Is one
concept doing several unrelated jobs? Is historical baggage posing as a
requirement? Is the code reproducing the shape of an earlier implementation
rather than the shape of the problem? Can an invariant replace a branch, a
constraint replace an instruction, a deletion replace a subsystem?

Do not refactor bloat into more aesthetically pleasing bloat.

### 4. Keep essential complexity, attack the accidental kind

Some complexity belongs to reality: real concurrency, external failure modes,
protocol semantics, distributed state, security boundaries. Keep it. Pretending
it away is not simplification, it is a bug with good manners.

Everything else, attack: duplicated representations, adapters between things
that should already speak the same language, speculative abstractions,
defensive handling of impossible states, configuration that configures
configuration, and wrappers with no semantic responsibility. The goal is not
minimal code at any cost. It is minimal *accidental* complexity.

### 5. Prefer invariants over instructions

If something must never happen, do not rely on documentation, convention,
prompts or discipline to prevent it. Make it structurally impossible.
Permissions over warnings. Schemas over prose. Types over comments. Separate
processes over behavioural instructions. A rule that has to be remembered is
weaker than a system that cannot break it.

### 6. Separate intelligence from authority

> The model proposes. The harness disposes.

Reasoning capability and execution authority are different things. The model
may reason as broadly as it likes; its authority stays narrow, explicit and
enforced from outside. Gates, permissions, repository protection and deployment
controls live outside the model's discretion, and the model does not get to
weaken them because it can argue convincingly about them. Intelligence works
inside strong boundaries. It does not replace them.

Make those boundaries obvious: authority, ownership, where data enters, validation,
persistence, external effects, irreversible operations and trust transitions.
Centralise each where it can be understood and enforced, rather than spreading it
through the codebase, and keep things simple inside it.

### 7. Decompose by meaning, not by file size

A component deserves to exist when it owns one coherent concept, invariant or
transition. You should be able to describe it in one precise sentence. If the
description needs a paragraph of unrelated "and also"s, it is several
components wearing one coat. Many small files that leave the conceptual
coupling untouched are not decomposition. They are confetti.

### 8. Search upstream for the shared cause

When several symptoms appear, do not assume several bugs. Ask: *what is the
smallest upstream cause that explains the largest number of downstream
observations?* Several awkward implementations usually mean one wrong
abstraction. Several failures usually mean one broken invariant. If component B
is awkward because component A exposes the wrong concept, fix A and delete the
compensation in B.

### 9. Make the representation do the work

Choose data structures, schemas and state machines that make correct behaviour
the natural behaviour. A good representation *removes* code. If a lot of logic
exists only to interpret or repair the representation, the representation is
wrong. Keep one canonical form. Keep derived information derived. If two pieces
of state must be kept in sync, first ask why there are two, because the best
synchronisation mechanism is usually deleting one of them.

### 10. Do not add generality without evidence

No plugin systems for plugins nobody has written. No interface for its one
implementation. No configuration for a case nobody has. Generalise when two
real instances reveal their shared structure, not when one imagined future
consumer might appreciate it.

### 11. Treat existing code adversarially

Existing *behaviour* may be required. Existing *structure* is not. Separate
externally observable behaviour and genuine invariants from historical
workarounds and obsolete assumptions. Every existing abstraction has to keep
earning its place. Sunk effort is not an argument. Neither is a passing test,
because a test verifies the implementation we happened to build. It does not
prove that implementation should exist.

### 12. Global simplicity beats local elegance

A helper can be beautiful while the system is incoherent. The recurring failure
in software is making every component locally tidy, defensive, reusable and
complete while the whole becomes incomprehensible. Judge each decision at
repository scale. Does it add a concept, a source of truth, a lifecycle, an
authority holder, another place state can diverge? Or does it just move the
complexity somewhere you are not looking?

## The operating system already solved this

A mature operating system, filesystem, language runtime and version-control
system embody decades of work on composition, isolation, persistence,
concurrency and observability. Use them before building weaker copies inside
the codebase.

**The filesystem is a state primitive.** A file can be human-readable
configuration, machine-readable configuration, durable state, an audit
surface, a diff, a trigger and a synchronisation boundary, all at once, and
every ordinary tool already knows how to handle it. Do not hide a direct
filesystem transition behind three layers of repository classes because it
feels "low level". Read the file, transform the data, write the file, and
respect atomicity where it actually matters.

**Git is part of the state machine.** It is not a developer tool that sits
outside the application. A branch holds proposed state. A commit is an
immutable description of a transition. The diff says exactly what changed.
Integration is acceptance. The default branch is accepted desired state, and
deployment realises it. That gives you provenance, rollback, inspection,
ordering and synchronisation from machinery that already exists and already
works. Do not rebuild it in an application database because someone once said
"Git is not a database". Understand the guarantees and use them deliberately.

**Change the source of truth, not every consumer of it.** If changing the model
for a rhythm is conceptually a configuration change, it is a configuration
change: edit the YAML, commit it, let the normal path apply it. Not a runtime
override table, a model registry or a parallel control plane.

**Prefer the language.** In Python that means `functools`, `itertools`,
`collections`, `pathlib`, generators, context managers and the sort you
already have, before any home-made infrastructure. Think in transformations
where you can (input, filter, map, reduce, output) and keep explicit state for
the parts of reality that are actually stateful.

The [representation example](engineering-doctrine-example.md) walks through the
classic case: a task that wanted to be a database row, an ORM model, a status
column and a sync job, and turned out to be a file in Git.

## Before you delete anything, ask two questions

"If I delete this, what concrete required behaviour becomes impossible?" is the
right question. It comes too late if you skip these two.

**Is it an invariant at all?** Much of what a codebase enforces is a performance
wish, a tidiness habit or a fear, written in the grammar of a rule so nobody
argues with it. "A withdrawn task must stop its running gate" reads like
correctness. It isn't. The requirement is that withdrawn work must not *land*.
Whether the gate finishes first is a question about wasted CPU, and wasted CPU
is not an invariant.

**Does the representation already hold it?** An invariant can be held by
design or by code, and only one of those needs maintenance. If withdrawal is
checked by the one writer that can push, nothing else has to check it. The
same invariant held by a status column needs a predicate at every stage that
might act, plus a recovery pass for rows whose process died. That code is the
price of choosing a representation that does not hold the invariant.

An invariant that survives both questions gets code. One that fails the first
was never real. One that fails the second is telling you the fact lives in the
wrong place, so move the fact instead of writing the check.

## Demolish, then fill

We call this *stormbeslå*. It is the one method here we will defend against
anyone.

Do not refactor by editing small pieces. The failure is structural, not a lack
of discipline: a small edit has no constraint on its own size, so each one is
locally defensible while the total grows. That is exactly how a well-behaved
session leaves every commit green, every decision reasonable, and the source
seven hundred lines *larger* than it started.

So invert it. Pick a whole concept, not a convenient file. Delete it
everywhere: the store, the module, its callers, its synchronisation, its
recovery path and the tests that only protect that machinery. Leave a hole with
the replacement primitive written on the rim. Do that everywhere in the concept
before you fill anything. Now the holes are visible, the line count has already
fallen, and no fill can quietly cost more than what it replaced, because what
it replaced is a number you can read.

- A hole is filled by a primitive, or it is not filled. If the fill turns out to
  be another module, name the primitive it embodies or revert it. If it
  recreates the subsystem you just removed, the representation is still wrong.
- Never leave half a workflow on the old representation and half on the new,
  joined by a synchroniser. That synchroniser is the bug.
- Do not polish code that is about to be deleted.
- A deletion is not finished until everything that described the removed thing is
  gone too. Prompt text that points at removed machinery is worse than silence: the
  model reconciles it against the filesystem and guesses. After a removal, re-read
  the whole prompt surface and every document that names it.
- Do not take a line budget. A budget is an instruction, and instructions get
  satisfied by compressing syntax, which is not the same as removing a concept.

The measure is semantic compression: fewer ideas needed to explain the same
correct system. Count concepts, independent facts, state transitions, authority
holders and execution paths. Report source size as a symptom, never as the goal.
A fact moved from SQLite into a pile of JSON files has not disappeared, it has
just lost its transactions. A move into Git pays only when Git's own
representation removes a second truth and the code that maintained it.

### The convergence check

During a structural refactor, every few commits hand the diff to a separate,
read-only reviewer (a model is fine) along with this page. It must not edit or
run the suite. It answers from the diff, not from the implementer's summary:
which concept disappeared, which primitive now owns the behaviour, and how the
number of independent representations changed. `scripts/converging.sh` prints
the arithmetic.

Call it **drifting** when source rises, a new module names no primitive, a
responsibility merely moved, one subsystem replaced another, or a green suite is
the only evidence offered. Two of those at once means **stop**, and name the
first change to reconsider.

## Tests protect invariants, not implementations

Tests should establish externally meaningful behaviour. A test whose only job is
to preserve incidental structure makes improvement harder, and when you delete
something and a test fails, first decide which kind it was.

A passing suite must say what it establishes. Local Git and SQLite fixtures do
not prove that a deployed steward can authenticate, prepare its native
workspace and complete a rhythm under its real service identity. A green macOS
run says nothing whatsoever about a Linux UID boundary. A failure test must
reach the boundary it names and fail for *that* reason; an unrelated
`TypeError` under an expected-failure marker proves nothing. Test totals are not
evidence. Carrying an old total forward to a new revision is worse than
reporting none.

Work from the operator journey downward: message in, work retained, candidate
accepted, exact revision gated and published, release healthy, result
delivered. Assert those facts at their real boundaries, with focused checks for
the failure and authority edges that remain. Fixture convenience is no reason to
keep an otherwise unused production admission or completion API alive. A full
suite is an integration check, not the definition of a working steward.

Evidence is the work product, ceremony is not. Repeated test selection, isolated
exports, hash ledgers, parallel reviews and per-slice documentation are not the
default. Isolate a run when concurrent edits would actually invalidate its evidence,
not as a ritual for every edit, and do not rerun checks on an already verified,
independent change just to attach another commit hash to it.

## Challenge the premise

A task description is not necessarily a correct decomposition of the problem.
When asked to add another handler, state, service, option or edge-case patch,
first find out whether the mechanism should exist. It is allowed, and expected,
to answer:

> This should not be built as requested, because a simpler upstream change
> removes the need for it.

Then explain the structural reason and build the simpler thing, if it preserves
what was actually wanted.

## Warning signs

Treat these as signs the model is wrong, not as the cost of doing business:

- several modules translate between near-identical shapes of the same data;
- comments explain why apparently impossible things can happen;
- abstractions exist mainly to coordinate other abstractions;
- configuration options interact combinatorially;
- tests need extensive mocking of internal machinery;
- several components can mutate the same state;
- correctness depends on an execution order nothing enforces;
- security depends on model obedience;
- a simple feature touches many unrelated places;
- deleting one component requires understanding all of them.

## When unsure, prefer

Fewer concepts, states, sources of truth, authority holders, lifecycles and
irreversible transitions. Stronger invariants, narrower interfaces, clearer
ownership. Not necessarily fewer lines: a ten-line abstraction that introduces
three new concepts can be worse than twenty explicit lines using concepts the
system already has.

## The final question

> What can I understand more deeply so that I no longer need to build this?

The system is finished when it is easier to explain than the pile of details it
is made from. If understanding it means memorising exceptions, it is not
finished. If a newcomer must first learn hundreds of incidental facts, the model
is probably wrong. And if improving the model makes a lot of code disappear,
improve the model.

The ideas above have ancestors, and we are happy to name them:
[a nod to the ancestors](doctrine-ancestry.md).
